newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Imports slowdown threatens Yugo industry growth.
newsitem.headline: Imports slowdown threatens Yugo industry growth.

text.p: The slowdown in imports towards the end of last year and early this year will have a negative effect on Yugoslavia's industrial production and exports, the Institute for Foreign Trade said in its latest report.

"Existing stocks could influence February results to an extent, but if the downward trend in imports continues, a further slowdown in industrial output in March will be inevitable," institute director Radovan Kovacevic said.
Industry was still slightly active thanks to reserves of raw materials and semi-manufactured goods created late last year, but signs of exhaustion are increasingly obvious, Kovacevic said.
Around 35 percent of last year's imports were raw materials, crude oil, copper ore and concentrates, petrol and wheat -- all products of a lower level of processing.
Industrial growth has been on the decline since last October with January output 20.8 percent lower than in December, mainly attributed to seasonal factors.
However January year-on-year output rose 2.9 percent.
According to official statistics, the 1996 trade deficit of $2.26 billion widened by another $191 million in January.
The gap is believed to have been financed mainly from unofficial accounts abroad to which funds were removed when sanctions were imposed on Yugoslavia in 1992.
January imports dropped to $323 million from $396 in December, while exports fell to $132 million from $168 million the previous month.
Lack of turnover capital in the country and funds from abroad remain the main obstacles to more dynamic production activity, the report said.
"Last year high interest rates in the country attracted some short-term credits, but now foreign partners are demanding fulfilment of export obligations from 1996," Kovacevic said.
Among last year's exports, raw materials and lightly processed goods such as ferrous metals, food and chemicals remained dominant.
January's exports followed last year's trend with raw materials accounting for 35 percent, followed by food and livestock at 16 percent.

Germany remained Yugoslavia's top trading partner, with total January trade worth $53 million, of which $41 million were imports. Italy was next with trade worth $46 million, of which $27 million were imports, followed by Russia, the Bosnian Serb Republic and Macedonia.
The bulk of the trade deficit in January, or $92 million, was with developed countries.
The institute also published data on wheat exports last year, which it said were worth $54 million and were primarily to Bulgaria, France, Romania and Russia.

According to the report, socially-owned firms accounted for 40 percent of last year's exports and 37 percent of imports. Private firms made up 23 percent of exports and 29 of imports, and those of mixed ownership 35 and 28 percent.
"This indicates that private and mixed sectors are slowly taking over domination in foreign trade," Kovacevic said. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 2224305
